summary: perf records raw performance numbers for each commit that lands on the product repos' main branches. In v0 it only builds a history of numbers, so that later versions can alert on regressions and bisect them.

how_it_works.title: Three measurements
how_it_works.text: The perf workflow measures innernet's Next.js build output size, xo-space's server start time over 5 starts, and innernet's search latency on a demo build with a fixed committed index. Builds and benchmarks run through the recipes repo's adapters on pinned Python, Node and pnpm versions.

how_it_works.title: Polling main, one commit per run
how_it_works.text: The workflow runs every 30 minutes and, for each measurement, takes the newest commit on main that has no record yet. Every commit since the oldest record is owed one, a backlog drains one commit per run, and a commit that fails three times is given up.

how_it_works.title: Raw records on a data branch
how_it_works.text: Each record is appended as a JSON Lines entry to this repo's perf-data branch, one file per repo and metric, with its unit and runner type. Lines are never edited and a commit gets at most one ok record.

how_it_works.title: Split trust between jobs
how_it_works.text: The measure job runs product code with read access only and uploads a ledger; the store job runs no product code and accepts only valid records for commits still pending before pushing perf-data. A separate perf-publish workflow then turns those records into results bundles for the test-pipelines results store.

status.text: Build-size records for innernet and the two benchmarks are merged and recording. The numbers are a record, not a regression signal: one measurement per commit on shared runners with no baseline, so nothing alerts or gates on them in v0.

perf polls main on a schedule rather than running inside each product repo's post-submit, which is still a TODO. Records can lag when main lands faster than one commit per 30-minute run, and commits that landed before a metric's first record are not owed one.
Whoever can push to perf-data or create a tag named main could still publish numbers until rulesets protect both.
